What you learned
How to build a centralized logging pipeline with Elasticsearch, Kibana, and Filebeat
How to collect logs from multiple containers running on macOS or Windows, where Docker hides its
internal log paths
How to apply the log-file-volume workaround: containerized apps write logs into a shared mounted
folder, and Filebeat tails those files to forward them to Elasticsearch
How to configure Filebeat inputs for each log source and enrich every log event with identifying
metadata, such as service.name, enabling clear separation and filtering in Kibana
How to explore logs in Kibana Discover, create data views, and run queries such as service.name :
"node-api" or message : "ERROR"
Why Docker metadata fields such as container.name aren't available on Docker Desktop, and how to
add meaningful replacements
How this Filebeat pattern stays fully compatible with Linux hosts, where Filebeat can alternatively read
Docker's native JSON log files directly
With these steps, you now understand how to centralize and search logs from diverse containerized applications
on any operating system, and how to adapt your approach when working with Docker Desktop or full Linux
environments.
Collecting and scraping metrics with Prometheus
In the previous section, we i d x _ d 6 9 f c b 2 c learned how to ship and centralize application logs. Logs tell us what happened, but not
how the system behaves over time. For that, we need metrics, numerical indicators that measure performance,
resource usage, and business activity.
In this section, we will use Prometheus, the most widely used open source metrics and alerting toolkit. Prometheus
works on a pull model: it regularly scrapes data from applications that expose their metrics on an HTTP endpoint
(usually /metrics).
To demonstrate how easy it is to i d x _ 3 e b 9 a 8 e a integrate Prometheus into any i d x _ 5 5 f 3 3 d c c language, we will create three tiny microservices,
written i d x _ a a 3 c 6 b 3 1 in Go, Python, and C# (.NET), each exposing a counter that tracks how many requests it has processed.
Step 1 – Preparing the project structure
Create a new i d x _ 4 c 1 d 2 5 3 e working folder with subdirectories for each service and Prometheus:
$ mkdir prometheus-demo && cd prometheus-demo
$ mkdir go-service py-service cs-service prometheus

Step 2 – Implementing the Go service
Go has excellent i d x _ 3 8 a 9 0 4 7 9 first-class i d x _ 0 1 3 8 0 e a 0 Prometheus support through the prometheus/client_golang library. Create a go-
service/main.go file with this content:
package main
import (
"fmt"
"net/http"
"github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus"
"github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/promhttp"
)
var reqCounter = prometheus.NewCounter(
prometheus.CounterOpts{
Name: "go_requests_total",
Help: "Total number of requests",
},
)
func main() {
prometheus.MustRegister(reqCounter)
http.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter,
r *http.Request) {
reqCounter.Inc()
fmt.Fprintf(w, "Hello from Go service!")
})
http.Handle("/metrics", promhttp.Handler())
http.ListenAndServe(":8081", nil)
}
The code defines a simple web server with two REST endpoints. The first one, "/", will return a hello message,
while the second one, "/metrics", will return the metrics ready for Prometheus to scrape. The web server listens to
incoming messages on port 8081.
Add a i d x _ 3 1 4 a b c 8 1 Dockerfile, go-service/Dockerfile, with i d x _ 6 f 0 7 6 6 2 e this content:
FROM golang:1.23-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go mod init go-service && go mod tidy && \
go build -o app

WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /src/app .

Step 3 – Implementing the Python service
Similar to the Go i d x _ 6 d a 4 1 0 7 e service, this Python service defines a i d x _ 6 f c 2 6 a 4 6 web server with the same endpoints, '/' and '/metrics'.
The web server listens on port 8082. The service uses Flask and the prometheus_client package. Add a py-
service/app.py file and give it this content:
from flask import Flask
from prometheus_client import Counter, generate_latest
from prometheus_client import CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST
import logging, sys
app = Flask(__name__)
# Enable unbuffered logging to stdout
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.INFO)
# Define a simple counter
counter = Counter('py_requests_total',
'Total HTTP requests handled')
@app.route('/')
def home():
counter.inc()
app.logger.info("Handled request to /")
return 'Hello from Python!'
@app.route('/metrics')
def metrics():
return generate_latest(), 200, {
'Content-Type': CONTENT_TYPE_LATEST}
if __name__ == '__main__':
app.logger.info("Starting Flask app on port 8082")
app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=8082)

Monitoring a containerized application
Monitoring a containerized i d x _ b a a 4 1 6 d 2 application is critical for understanding its health, resource consumption, and overall
performance. In this section, we will modernize our approach using the latest versions i d x _ d 2 9 1 1 3 a 8 of Prometheus, Node
Exporter, and Grafana, three of the most i d x _ c 7 a 8 2 b 2 d popular i d x _ 3 c 2 5 4 e d 5 open source tools for metrics and visualization.
By following this step-by-step exercise, you will set up a complete monitoring stack that collects metrics from a
running containerized service and visualizes them in Grafana dashboards.
Step 1 – Preparing the folder structure
Before we can start, let's i d x _ 3 4 f 2 a 7 d e organize our project files so that each tool has its own folder. Create a new subfolder in

chunks.content:
Chapter 12 412
How to instrument an application to expose Prometheus metrics
How to visualize metrics and build custom dashboards
How to optionally configure alerts to act proactively
With our monitoring stack now in place, we can collect detailed metrics, visualize them in Grafana dashboards,
and even set up alerts for early warnings. Yet, effective monitoring is only one part of a broader picture. To truly
understand and protect our containerized systems, we need to move beyond metrics alone and look at
observability and security monitoring.
Observability and security monitoring
So far, we have looked at how to collect logs, ship them to a central location, scrape metrics, and visualize them in
dashboards. This is the foundation of running containerized applications in production. However, true
observability i d x _ b 6 e f e 2 b 5 goes beyond logs and metrics. It combines logs, metrics, and traces, often called the three pillars of
observability:
Logs give you i d x _ 1 8 9 e 3 6 3 7 detailed, event-level information
Metrics provide i d x _ 9 6 f f a 5 a 6 aggregated numbers that show trends and patterns
Traces allow i d x _ a c 8 1 b 3 e 2 you to follow a single request as it travels through multiple services
Together, they let you answer not just what happened, but also why it happened. In containerized and distributed
systems, this level of insight is essential.
Security is another important dimension. Containers generate their own unique risks, for example, running as root,
vulnerable dependencies in images, or unexpected network connections. Monitoring i d x _ 5 c d 4 d 3 3 c systems can help detect these
issues early:
Image scanning tools (such as Docker Scout, Trivy, or Snyk) can detect known vulnerabilities before
containers are even deployed
Runtime monitoring (for example, with Falco or Sysdig) can alert you when a container process behaves
in suspicious ways, such as spawning a shell inside a web server container
Audit logs from Docker or Kubernetes can be shipped to your central logging solution to provide a record
of who did what and when
While a full observability stack (logs, metrics, traces) and dedicated security monitoring solutions are often
introduced at the orchestrator level (Kubernetes), it is useful to understand already at this stage that monitoring is
not just about performance. It is about the health, reliability, and security of your applications and infrastructure.
Summary
In this chapter, we moved beyond simply running containers and learned how to observe and understand them in
operation. We began by exploring Docker's built-in logging system and configuration options such as log drivers,
rotation, and retention. We then built a practical, cross-platform logging pipeline using the Elastic Stack, with
Filebeat as a lightweight log shipper that collects container logs and sends them to Elasticsearch.

Special attention was given to differences between Linux and Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows. On Linux,
Filebeat can read Docker's JSON log files directly. On macOS and Windows, we applied a volume-based
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
413 Shipping Logs and Monitoring Containers
workaround: applications write their logs to a shared folder that Filebeat tails. This approach made our setup work
consistently on every platform.
With Kibana, we learned how to explore, filter, and visualize logs, enriching them with useful metadata such as
service.name to make multi-service debugging easy.
We then shifted focus from logs to metrics using Prometheus, instrumenting three small microservices written in
Go, Python, and C#. We configured Prometheus to scrape metrics from those services and visualized them in
Grafana, building dashboards and basic alerts that track container health and performance over time.
Finally, we introduced the broader concept of observability, where logs, metrics, and traces together form a
complete picture of system behavior. Observability gives you the data to detect issues early, understand root causes
quickly, and verify the effect of changes.
In the next chapter, we will build on this foundation by addressing the security dimension of container operations.
You will learn how to secure the entire container lifecycle, from image creation to runtime, by scanning for
vulnerabilities, enforcing image trust, hardening configurations, managing secrets, and detecting anomalies at
runtime.
Questions
Here are a few questions that you should try to answer to self-assess your learning progress:
Why is centralized logging important in containerized environments?
What role does Filebeat play in the Elastic Stack?
Why can't Filebeat read Docker logs directly on macOS and Windows?
How does the shared-volume logging workaround function?
What is the benefit of adding custom fields such as service.name in Filebeat's configuration?
How do logs and metrics differ?
What does Prometheus do, and how does it collect data?
What is Grafana's role in the monitoring stack?
Why did the chapter use three different languages (Go, Python, and C#) in the Prometheus example?
What is observability, and how is it different from monitoring?
How does observability help with container security?
What's the main takeaway from this chapter before moving on to container security?

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 414
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 414
Answers
Here are some sample answers to the questions for this chapter:
Because containers are ephemeral and often run across multiple hosts, their local logs can disappear
when containers stop or are redeployed. Centralized logging aggregates all logs in one place, making it
possible to search, correlate, and analyze events across different containers and services.
Filebeat acts as a lightweight log shipper. It collects logs from files or containers, optionally enriches
them with metadata, and forwards them to Elasticsearch for indexing and analysis in Kibana.
On macOS and Windows, Docker runs inside a lightweight Linux VM, so the / var/lib/docker/
containers path (where Docker stores logs) is not accessible from the host. Filebeat, therefore, can't read
those files directly. The workaround is to have containers write logs to a shared mounted volume, which
Filebeat tails from the host side.
Each container writes its log output to a file inside a shared volume (for example, / usr/src/app/logs).
Filebeat mounts the same volume in read-only mode and tails those files, shipping log lines to
Elasticsearch. This makes the setup portable across Linux, macOS, and Windows.
Adding service.name (and similar fields) enriches each log event with clear context. It allows you to
filter and query logs per service in Kibana, compensating for the lack of Docker metadata on macOS and
Windows.
Logs describe discrete events—what happened and when—while metrics provide continuous, numeric
measurements of system behavior (such as CPU usage or request rate). Both are complementary: logs
help diagnose causes, and metrics help detect trends or anomalies.
Prometheus is an open source monitoring and alerting system. It pulls data from endpoints (usually /
metrics) exposed by applications or exporters, storing the results as time-series data for querying and
visualization.
Grafana visualizes metrics collected by Prometheus. It provides dashboards, charts, and alerting features
that make it easy to interpret numerical data and track application performance over time.
To demonstrate that Prometheus is language-agnostic. Any application that can expose metrics over
HTTP in the Prometheus format can be monitored, regardless of the programming language used.
Monitoring tracks known metrics and thresholds to detect when something goes wrong. Observability
goes deeper; it combines logs, metrics, and traces to understand why something went wrong, even for
unexpected failures. It's about gaining insight, not just visibility.
Observability provides the visibility needed to spot unusual behavior, such as unexpected network
activity or resource spikes. These can be early signs of compromise or misconfiguration. Effective
observability lays the foundation for detecting and responding to security incidents.

Securing Containers
In previous chapters, particularly chapters 4, 6, 7, and 11, we learned how to build, test, and monitor containerized
applications. We've also seen how containers can improve consistency, portability, and productivity throughout
the software supply chain. However, as container adoption grows, so does the attack surface. A single
misconfiguration or a vulnerable image can compromise an entire environment.
In this chapter, we will learn how to secure our containerized applications throughout their entire life cycle, from
image creation to runtime. We will discuss how to protect against supply chain risks, perform image scanning,
enforce content trust, apply container hardening practices, and manage secrets securely. Finally, we will explore
runtime security tools that can detect and respond to threats in real time.
Here is a list of topics we are going to discuss in this chapter:
Supply chain security
Image vulnerability scanning and content trust
Container hardening practices
Secrets management
Runtime security tools
After finishing this chapter, you will be able to do the following:
Generate and maintain a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) to track all components in container
images
Scan container images for vulnerabilities and enforce image signing for trust
Apply container hardening practices such as running containers as non-root users and using read-only
filesystems
Securely manage secrets with dedicated tools and environment configurations
Deploy runtime security tools to monitor container behavior and detect anomalies

Scout, Trivy, and Cosign. Optionally, tools such as grype, Syft, and Falco can be installed to follow the examples

Installing Trivy and Cosign on Windows
On Windows, you i d x _ a c 8 7 4 4 c 8 have several options for installing and running Trivy:
Option A: Use official binaries. Visit the Trivy releases page (on GitHub) or the Trivy installer docs.
Option B: Use WSL2. On Ubuntu, for example, use the following command to install Trivy:
curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/trivy/main/contrib/
install.sh | sh
Option C: Run Trivy inside a container:
docker run --rm \
-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
-v ~/.cache/trivy:/root/.cache/trivy \
aquasec/trivy image hello-ruby:latest
Similarly, you have i d x _ 3 2 a 8 1 9 2 d several options to install Cosign:
Option A: Use winget:
PS> winget install --id=Sigstore.Cosign -e
Option B: Use Chocolatey:
PS> choco install cosign
Verify the installation in your command prompt, such as PowerShell, with the following:
PS> cosign version
Now that we have installed all the prerequisites, let's dive into the details.
Supply chain security
When i d x _ 1 d 1 8 a 5 9 a we talk about security in the context of containers, we cannot limit ourselves to the running container alone.
A secure container starts long before it is ever executed; it begins at build time. Each container image is made up of
multiple layers, often inherited from other images that may themselves come from public registries or third-party
sources. Every one of those layers represents a potential entry point for malicious code, outdated libraries, or
hidden secrets.
The first step in securing containers is therefore to secure the software supply chain, the full path that software
takes from source code to a running container image in production.
In traditional software development, the supply chain was relatively short and predictable: developers wrote the
code, built it on their machines, and shipped binaries to operations. Containers changed that dramatically. Today, a

Chapter 13 420
single image can include hundreds of packages, each i d x _ 4 7 c f 7 c 9 3 maintained by different people or organizations and
distributed through different channels. Without proper visibility and control, you simply do not know what you
are running in production.
Understanding what makes up your image
To gain visibility into what is inside a container image, we use an SBOM. An i d x _ 7 e 1 8 d 0 6 1 SBOM is a detailed inventory listing all
components, libraries, and dependencies used to build a software artifact. Think of i d x _ 6 c 9 2 d f 4 f it as a manifest for your
container image.
Having an SBOM allows you to answer crucial questions such as the following:
Which open source packages and versions does my image include?
Which of those have known vulnerabilities?
Where do they come from, and under which licenses are they distributed?
In regulated industries, maintaining an SBOM is not just best practice; it is increasingly a compliance requirement.
Frameworks such as NIST SP 800-218 (the Secure Software Development Framework) and initiatives such as the
U.S. Executive Order 14028 emphasize the need for verifiable software provenance.
Let's generate our first SBOM for a sample image.
Generating an SBOM
The easiest i d x _ 7 4 6 7 6 c 8 f way to generate an SBOM for a container image is by using the open source tool Syft from Anchore. Syft
can create SBOMs in several standard formats, such as SPDX or CycloneDX.
Install it on macOS as follows:
$ brew install anchore/syft/syft
On Windows, use winget to install the tool:
$ winget install Anchore.Syft
Finally, on i d x _ 9 3 b a d 9 6 b Linux, we can use the following commands to install syft:
$ curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/syft/main/install.sh | sh
$ sudo mv syft /usr/local/bin/
Let's analyze the latest version of the official nginx image:
$ syft nginx:latest
You will see output similar to this:

Figure 13.1: BOM for the latest nginx Docker image
Note that the list of items is much longer but has been cut for readability.
Syft crawls through all layers of the image, identifies installed packages, and lists their metadata. You i d x _ c 6 4 4 c b 9 7 can also
export the SBOM in a machine-readable format for automated processing:
$ syft nginx:latest -o cyclonedx-json > nginx-sbom.json
This file can be stored alongside the image in your registry or attached as build metadata in your CI/CD pipeline.
Verifying image provenance
Once we i d x _ 4 b 4 8 a 7 c 6 know what is in our images, we must ensure those images actually come from a trusted source. Using
unsigned or tampered images is one of the most common supply chain risks.
Docker Engine supports i d x _ 0 f e e e b 9 e image signing and verification using tools such as Cosign (part of the Sigstore project).

Building and running the image
Now that we have i d x _ 5 3 9 3 1 9 6 c built a sample Ruby application, let's i d x _ e 3 9 3 0 2 1 d build and run it:
From inside the chapter-13/hello-ruby folder, run the following:
$ docker build -t hello-ruby:latest .

Generating a BOM and scanning the image
Before i d x _ d d 4 6 b f 9 7 signing, you might want to inspect the image contents:
$ syft hello-ruby:latest \
-o cyclonedx-json > hello-ruby-sbom.json
The preceding commands allow you to list all packages in your Docker image.
Scanning the image
You can also i d x _ 8 3 d 0 8 3 5 f scan the image for vulnerabilities:
$ trivy image hello-ruby:latest
This command allows you to check for i d x _ d 9 a b 9 7 c a known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). You can also
integrate that into your CI pipeline later.
Verifying and signing the image
Here is i d x _ 1 f 9 2 1 b a c how to build, verify, and sign a container i d x _ d b 7 7 d 4 9 4 image step by step:
Let's first tag the hello-ruby image and push it to Docker Hub:
$ docker image tag hello-ruby:latest \
<username>/hello-ruby:v1.0.0
$ docker login -u <username>
$ docker image push <username>/hello-ruby:v1.0.0

425 Securing Containers
For signing to work, the image needs to be pushed first to a repository such as Docker Hub, and ideally, it
should not have a floating tag such as latest. Thus, we will tag the image, log in to Docker Hub, and push
the image. Please use your username for Docker Hub instead of <username>.
Let's sign the image that we have built ourselves:
$ cosign generate-key-pair
$ cosign sign --key cosign.key \
<username>/hello-ruby:v1.0.0
The first command generates a public/private key pair. The second signs the image with your private key.
You can verify the signature later with the following:
$ cosign verify --key cosign.pub \
<username>/hello-ruby:v1.0.0
If verification succeeds, you can be confident that the image has not been altered since you built it and that it
indeed comes from you or your organization.
Once you've i d x _ 2 b d 0 3 d 2 e followed these steps, you are ready to i d x _ e f 4 e b 7 6 f enforce that only signed, verified images are allowed in your
deployments. In the next section, we'll explore how to integrate image signing into your CI/CD pipeline and how to
enforce verification in your runtime environment.
Securing the pipeline
A secure supply chain i d x _ 9 1 4 f 2 5 b 3 is not limited to images and signatures. We must also ensure that every step in our build
pipeline, from source control to CI/CD and the registry, is protected.
Here are some best practices to keep in mind:
Always use version-pinned base images (for example, python:3.12-alpine) instead of floating tags such
as latest
Use private registries for internal images and restrict access via authentication and role-based policies
Enforce multi-stage Docker builds to prevent build-time secrets or tools from leaking into the final image
Run image builds on isolated runners that are regularly patched and have no unnecessary internet access
Continuously monitor dependencies and rebuild images when new vulnerabilities are disclosed
Once we establish trust in our supply chain and can prove what goes into every image, we can move to the next
logical step, which is analyzing and scanning those images for vulnerabilities.
Image vulnerability scanning and content trust
Once we have built an image and generated an SBOM, our next line of defense is to scan the image for known i d x _ 8 b c 3 0 3 d f
vulnerabilities, and then enforce that only trusted, signed images i d x _ a 8 0 f 5 c 5 1 make it into production. In this section, we'll
cover the following:
Why vulnerability scanning matters

A walk-through using Trivy
Understanding scoring, severity levels, ignoring, and allow-listing
Introducing content trust via Cosign and Sigstore
Enforcing signed images at runtime (CI/CD and deployment)
Let's get started.
Why scan container images?
Every i d x _ d a 2 2 b a f d container image includes OS packages, language libraries, and dependencies, many of which you didn't write
yourself. These third-party components may carry known vulnerabilities, that is, CVEs. Without scanning, you risk
shipping exploitable code into production.
There are some key reasons for vulnerability scanning:
Early detection: Catching security flaws before runtime reduces the blast radius
Compliance flagging: Many regulations require known vulnerabilities to be controlled
Continuous hygiene: Images must be rescanned regularly, as new CVEs are discovered
Policy gating: You can set rules such as " no image with critical CVEs may be deployed "
A popular tool in the open source ecosystem is Trivy (from Aqua Security), which is fast and simple and can scan
container images (among other artifacts) for OS and library vulnerabilities.
Let's walk through using it with our hello-ruby image.
Scanning with Trivy
Here's a i d x _ c 7 c e 1 5 8 3 step-by-step guide to scan the hello-ruby image i d x _ 2 a e 2 3 f f d you built earlier:
Make sure you have installed Trivy as described earlier in the Technical requirements section.
Run the following command to scan the hello-ruby image:
$ trivy image hello-ruby:latest
You should get a fairly long output that lists vulnerabilities by package and severity (e.g. CRITICAL, HIGH,
MEDIUM), as well as a risk summary.
Interpret the report. This scan will show the following:
Package name and version
Vulnerability ID (CVE number)
Severity level
Fixed version (if available)
Links to advisory or description

Let's address failing to build or exit codes. Trivy supports returning a non-zero exit code if vulnerabilities
exceed certain thresholds. Here is an example:
$ trivy image hello-ruby:latest \
--severity CRITICAL,HIGH \
--exit-code 1
This i d x _ 2 1 b 8 7 6 b b causes i d x _ 3 0 f 8 5 3 a 0 the process to fail if any CRITICAL or HIGH vulnerabilities are found, which is useful in CI
pipelines.
If you need to export output in machine formats, you can produce JSON, SARIF, or formatted outputs to
integrate into dashboards:
$ trivy image hello-ruby:latest \
-f json -o trivy-result.json
Remember to re-scan regularly. Trivy maintains a vulnerability database (trivy-db) and updates it. On
the first run, it will download or refresh. On subsequent runs, it can reuse cached data to speed up scans.
You may choose to ignore specific CVEs (for example, false positives or mitigated issues) via ignore lists
or allow lists, but do so judiciously.
At this point, you should have a clear view of potential vulnerabilities in hello-ruby:latest.
Content trust: cryptographic guarantees via Cosign
Scanning i d x _ 4 a 3 9 b 8 c a alone is i d x _ e 6 3 8 e 9 d 9 not enough. Even if you scanned an image, someone might push a tampered version or
substitute a malicious image with the same tag. That's where content trust comes in: tying the image to a
cryptographic signature that you can verify.
Modern i d x _ d e d 6 c c 8 f container signing is largely done using Cosign, which is part of the Sigstore project. Cosign supports i d x _ 2 d 9 0 e b 6 0 the
following:
Signing container images (or related artifacts)
Key management (local keys, KMS, hardware, OIDC, keyless flows)
Verification of signatures
Transparency logs and auditability
Here's how we integrate Cosign into our workflow for the hello-ruby application.

Chapter 13 428
Signing and verifying with Cosign
Let's tie i d x _ 9 5 6 2 1 1 9 b everything together:
Install Cosign as i d x _ 9 1 8 2 c 1 c e described in this chapter's Technical requirements section.
Generate a key pair:
$ cosign generate-key-pair
This will output cosign.key (private) and cosign.pub (public) files.
Sign the image:
$ cosign sign --key cosign.key \
<username>/hello-ruby:v1.0.0
Cosign will attach a signature to the image and push that signature into the registry (or local store,
depending on flags).
Verify the signature:
$ cosign verify –key cosign.pub \
<username>/hello-ruby:v1.0.0
If successful, you will see something like this:
Verified OK : <username>/hello-ruby:v1.0.0
Cosign i d x _ 0 7 f 2 6 1 a b supports more advanced workflows (for example, keyless via OIDC, KMS-based, or storing cert
chains) without managing private keys yourself.
When i d x _ 1 d d 1 2 1 7 d signing, you can add annotations (key-value metadata), which can later be validated or used to
carry environment or build data:
$ cosign sign -a git-commit=abc123 \
--key cosign.key <username>/hello-ruby:v1.0.0
You can sign an image multiple times under different keys (e.g., for audit or separation of roles). You can
also rotate keys—but you must manage trust transitions carefully.
We have learned how to sign and verify a Docker image. Let's see how we can enforce it in our CI/CD pipelines.
Enforcing signing and verifying in CI/CD pipelines and at
runtime
Now that you i d x _ 6 5 e c e 1 8 e can scan and i d x _ 3 b d f 0 1 8 4 sign a Docker image, the final piece is enforcement:
In your CI pipeline, make vulnerability scanning a gate: if the image fails the scan, the pipeline stops.

Also require signature verification in the pipeline or as part of a deployment step.
At runtime (for example, Kubernetes admission controllers or container runtimes), enforce that only
signed images are accepted. Tools i d x _ 3 c 2 4 a 8 9 c such as Connaisseur, Cosign policy admission controllers, and built-
in Kubernetes Gatekeeper policies can validate signatures before Pods are allowed.
In registries that support content trust (for example, Harbor with Cosign integration), you can require
that images must be signed before being pulled.
By i d x _ f f 7 e 8 0 4 f combining i d x _ 1 d a 0 6 7 0 a scanning, signing, and enforcement, you build a defense-in-depth strategy: even if a vulnerability
slips through, an unsigned or tampered image cannot enter production.
Container hardening practices
Even after i d x _ 6 7 6 5 1 3 4 3 securing your supply chain and ensuring image trust, your containers still run with defaults that may
expose you to risk. Hardening is the practice of tightening devices, filesystems, privileges, and runtime constraints
to reduce the attack surface and mitigate damage if something does go wrong.
In this section, we'll cover the following:
Principle of least privilege (running as non-root, dropping capabilities)
Using read-only filesystems, limited mounts, and minimal images
Applying seccomp, AppArmor, SELinux, and Linux kernel security features
Resource limits and sandboxing
Multi-stage builds and reducing image bloat
Health checks, monitoring, and defense in depth
We'll interleave practical Dockerfile snippets and container runtime options that you can apply immediately.
Principle of least privilege: run as non-root and drop capabilities
By i d x _ 8 a 8 2 5 e 3 e default, many images (including official ones) run i d x _ c 6 7 7 8 0 4 2 as root inside the container. If a process escapes or is
compromised within the container, running as root gives it far more leverage. We want to reduce what that process
can do.
Adding a non-root user in your Dockerfile
Here's how you i d x _ 7 c 2 d 6 c 8 1 can modify your Dockerfile (for the Ruby app or any app) to switch to a non-root user:

Chapter 13 430
Figure 13.6: Switching to a non-root user
Here are some notes:
groupadd -r and useradd -r create a system (non-login) user and group
We change ownership so our app files are accessible to that user
We switch to USER appuser before the final commands
Any file i d x _ f 0 b c 8 4 5 3 writes by your app must go to directories that the non-root user can write to (so avoid writing to
root-owned directories)
Dropping unnecessary Linux capabilities
Even a i d x _ 8 d a 0 3 2 f b non-root container process might have extra Linux capabilities (for example, CAP_NET_ADMIN or
CAP_SYS_PTRACE) that are not needed. It's safer to strip them out.
At runtime, you can run the following:
$ docker run --rm \
-p 4567:4567 \
--cap-drop ALL \
--cap-add CHOWN \
--cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
hello-ruby:latest
Note the following here:
--cap-drop ALL removes all capabilities initially
--cap-add selectively adds only those you need (for example, to bind to low ports, change file ownership,
and so on)
If your app doesn't need a capability, don't include it.

Using --no-new-privileges
This i d x _ 6 a 4 2 8 d a 7 flag ensures that even if a process tries to escalate privileges (for example, via setuid or kernel exploit), it
cannot gain new ones beyond what's already present:
$ docker run --rm \
-p 4567:4567 \
--no-new-privileges \
hello-ruby:latest
This is i d x _ d c 4 1 f 9 b 8 simple but powerful; it enforces that no process in the container may gain additional privileges.
These practices—non-root, drop capabilities, and no-new-privileges —go a long way in limiting the potential of
damage.
Read-only filesystems, immutable layers, and minimal mounts
One of the i d x _ 8 c 8 e f 7 e 8 strongest constraints is to make as much of the container filesystem as possible read-only, and only
mount what absolutely must be writable.
Mounting your container rootfs as read-only
At i d x _ 0 3 4 0 f 7 7 4 runtime, use this command:
$ docker run --rm \
-p 4567:4567 \
--read-only \
hello-ruby:latest
--read-only makes the container's root filesystem read-only. Any attempts to write outside volumes will fail.
Mounting specific directories as writable volumes
If your i d x _ f 0 4 0 0 e 2 6 application writes logs, temp files, uploads, and so on, mount just those directories:
$ docker run --rm \
-p 4567:4567 \
--read-only \
-v /usr/src/app/logs \
-v /usr/src/app/tmp \
hello-ruby:latest
Note that on macOS, --no-new-privileges is not available. You can use the following alternative
instead: --security-opt no-new-privilege:true.
Note

chunks.content:
Chapter 13 432
Using minimal images (scratch or distroless)
The fewer OS packages i d x _ 0 4 f 0 a 3 6 6 and utilities your image includes, the smaller your attack surface. Here are some
approaches to consider:
Use a slim or Alpine base image instead of ruby:latest
Use distroless images (with no shell, no package manager) where feasible
Delete unused files, documentation, package caches, and build tools in your final image
Use multi-stage builds to ensure that build-time dependencies (compilers, test suites, etc.) are not
included in the final runtime image
Here is an example multi-stage build snippet:
Figure 13.7: Multi-stage Dockerfiles
This i d x _ 7 5 2 5 6 e 5 5 way, intermediate layers (compilers and build caches) never appear in the final runtime image.
Kernel-level security: seccomp, AppArmor, SELinux, and user
namespaces
Your i d x _ f 1 d c 0 5 a 0 container runtime and host kernel provide mechanisms to impose extra constraints. You should leverage
them:
seccomp filters: Disable or restrict syscalls not needed by your container. Docker by default ships with a
default seccomp profile restricting many dangerous syscalls.
•
•
•
•
•
433 Securing Containers
AppArmor and SELinux: Provide security policies that restrict the filesystem and resource access of
containers, allowing you to assign specific security profiles to individual containers to further harden
their runtime behavior.
User namespaces: Remap container UIDs to non-root UIDs on the host, reducing risk if the i d x _ 4 c 3 9 b 7 c d container
tries to break out. Docker supports user namespace remapping.
Disable privileged mode: Never run with --privileged unless absolutely necessary.
Disable kernel capabilities: As covered in the Dropping unnecessary Linux capabilities section earlier in
this chapter.
Disable inter-container communication: Use --icc=false so one container cannot easily reach others
by default.
Here is an example:
$ docker run --rm \
-p 4567:4567 \
--security-opt seccomp=default.json \
--security-opt apparmor=my-profile \
hello-ruby:latest
You can generate or customize default.json to specify allowed syscalls.
Resource limits and cgroups
You should i d x _ b 3 1 a a c 7 5 constrain containers so they cannot exhaust host resources:
--memory: Cap memory usage
--cpus: Limit CPU share
--pids-limit: Limit number of processes
Also consider --ulimit flags for file descriptors and open files
These limits i d x _ 2 a b b c b d 3 help prevent runaway containers or denial-of-service attacks inside your container cluster.
Health checks, monitoring, and defense in depth
Hardening isn't just about preventing bad things; it's about detecting and recovering.
Adding a HEALTHCHECK statement to your Dockerfile
Always i d x _ 0 9 5 4 6 3 2 c add a HEALTHCHECK statement to your Dockerfile; for example, for our hello-ruby image, use the following:

$ HEALTHCHECK \
--interval=30s --timeout=5s \
--start-period=5s --retries=3 \
CMD curl -f http://localhost:4567/ || exit 1
This allows Docker (or any other orchestrator) to mark containers as unhealthy and restart them.

Logging and monitoring agent
Run a sidecar i d x _ 7 1 c c 8 3 f 9 or lightweight agent that tracks unexpected behavior, such as file changes or resource spikes. Later,
we'll cover runtime security tools such as Falco.
Immutable infrastructure mindset
If a i d x _ 9 c 1 8 2 5 0 c container is compromised or unhealthy, you should replace it instead of patching it in place.
Putting it all together: hardened example for hello-ruby
Here's a consolidated i d x _ 2 c 1 5 b 5 0 5 Dockerfile with hardening features:
Figure 13.8: Hardened Dockerfile for the hello-ruby application

$ docker run --rm \
-p 4567:4567 \
--read-only \
--cap-drop ALL \
--cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
--no-new-privileges \
--memory 256m \
--cpus 0.5 \

435 Securing Containers
At this point, note the following:
The container rootfs is read-only
Only the minimal capability (NET_BIND_SERVICE) is granted
The process cannot gain new privileges
CPU and memory are limited
The app runs as non-root
This is a strong baseline you can build on.

Secrets management
Once you've i d x _ 0 7 a 7 d b 7 6 locked down your supply chain and hardened your images, one of the most fragile points in container
security continues to be secrets—API keys, database passwords, TLS certificates, SSH keys, tokens, and so on. If
these leak, an attacker may bypass many of your defenses.
In this section, we'll cover the following:
Why you should never bake secrets into images or environment variables
Runtime secret injection techniques (Docker secrets, Compose, or Swarm)
•

437 Securing Containers
Build-time secrets (for private registries, credentials during a Docker build)

Best practices: rotation, least privilege, audit, mitigation
Let's dive in.
Why not bake secrets into your image or env vars?
A common (but dangerous) pattern is putting the following somewhere inside your Dockerfile or putting
credentials in your source code or config files:
ENV DB_PASSWORD="SuperSecret123"
These approaches are brittle for the following reasons:
Images are immutable and often cached or shared; the secret travels everywhere
Layers in the image may be inspected; someone with access to the registry or image can reverse-engineer

chunks.heading: Chapter 13 436
chunks.content:
secrets
Environment variables may leak (logs, debug dumps, or process listings)
If you ever change the secret, you must rebuild and redeploy everywhere
In fact, a 2023 study of public container images found that approximately 8.5% of images inadvertently included
leaked secrets, such as private keys or API tokens (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03958).
So, secrets should be treated separately from image builds and code, strictly controlled, and frequently rotated.
Runtime secret injection
Runtime secret injection i d x _ 5 8 1 f b d a 7 describes mechanisms that allow sensitive information, such as passwords or API keys, to
be securely provided to containers at runtime without baking them into images or configuration files, as
demonstrated by Docker Swarm and Docker Compose.
Docker Swarm and Docker secrets (for services)
Docker i d x _ 7 3 d 6 8 b b f has i d x _ 9 8 6 e 3 9 8 2 first-class support for secrets in Swarm mode. Secrets created in Swarm are encrypted at rest and in
transit and are exposed only to service containers that request them.
Here's how you can use them:
Initialize Swarm (if not already done):
$ docker swarm init
Create a secret: Suppose you have a file, db_password.txt, containing your password:
$ docker secret create db_password db_password.txt

Deploy a service that uses that secret: When you create (or update) a service, attach the secret:
$ docker service create \
--name myapp \
--secret db_password \
-e DB_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password \
myapp:latest
Inside each i d x _ 8 c c b b 9 c b container, the secret is i d x _ 3 a c 6 6 6 e 3 mounted to /run/secrets/db_password (by default).
Access the secret in your app: Rather than reading an environment variable, your app should read from
the file. The following is an example in Ruby:
password = File.read("/run/secrets/db_password").strip
Removing or rotating secrets: Docker does not support modifying the value of an existing secret in
place. Instead, you must create a new secret (for example, db_password_v2) and update the service to
remove the old one and attach the new one:
$ docker service update \
--secret-rm db_password \
--secret-add \
source=db_password_v2,target=db_password \
myapp
Once no service references the old secret, you can remove it:
$ docker secret rm db_password
Docker Compose and secrets
If you're i d x _ 8 3 c 6 5 4 e c not using full Swarm, Docker Compose (v3 and later) supports secrets, though it is less feature-rich than
Swarm. Secrets i d x _ c b 6 d 9 a 6 6 defined in docker-compose.yml are mounted into containers similarly.
Here's a minimal example:
services:
web:
image: hello-ruby:latest
secrets:
- db_password
environment:
DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
secrets:

When you run docker compose up, Docker Compose mounts the secret file inside the container at /run/secrets/
db_password. The app then reads from the file, not from ENV.
Be aware that Docker Compose secrets support is limited. It lacks rotation, Swarm-level encryption, and fine-
grained access controls.
Build-time secrets
Sometimes your i d x _ 4 2 a 2 f a 0 0 build process needs access to private dependencies (artifact repositories, private Git clones, and
APIs). But passing secrets via build arguments or environment variables is dangerous, because they may persist in
image layers. Docker's build secret support lets you mount secrets only for a particular build step and ensures they
are not kept in the final layers.
Here's how:
Pass the secret at build time.
In your Dockerfile, use RUN --mount=type=secret.
The secret is i d x _ 2 0 d f 1 6 0 4 exposed to that RUN layer as a file (for example, /run/secrets/repo_token), but it is not preserved in
later layers or the final image.
This pattern helps you fetch private artifacts securely during build without embedding credentials into your image.
External secret management (vault, cloud, and sidecars)
While Docker's i d x _ 5 5 b f 1 8 5 5 built-in secrets are useful in many cases, in sophisticated environments (such as cloud, multi-
tenant, and regulated systems), you often need a full secrets management system (such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS
Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager, and so on).
The general pattern is as follows:
Store secrets securely in the external system (with RBAC, auditing, and versioning).
At runtime or startup, your container (or a sidecar) fetches the required secret via an authenticated call
(OIDC, IAM role, or service principal).
The fetched secret is then passed to your application (via an in-memory file, environment variable, or
injected secret).
Rotate and revoke secrets centrally; containers fetch fresh versions when needed.
Using sidecars is a popular pattern in which i d x _ 5 a f a a 4 1 5 a small secrets injector container runs alongside the application
container, retrieves secrets from a secure source, and injects or updates them via a shared volume or memory buffer
without exposing credentials in the application code.
This pattern decouples secrets from code and images entirely, making rotation, access control, and auditing
simpler and safer.

Trade-offs and caveats
While runtime i d x _ b b 6 7 f 9 5 e secret injection significantly improves the security posture of containerized applications, it comes
with important trade-offs and limitations that must be understood before adopting it in production environments.
The main trade-offs i d x _ a 3 f a 2 8 a 1 include the following:
Docker secrets in Swarm only work when using services; you cannot use them with standalone docker
run containers.
Docker Compose secrets do not offer encryption at rest or audit capabilities.
Build-time secret mounts require Docker v1.4+ syntax and features as older Docker engines may not
support them.
Fetching secrets at runtime introduces an additional dependency during application startup, which may
result in a slight increase in startup time.
If your container is compromised, secrets injected into its memory or files might still be exfiltrated.
Secrets management reduces exposure, but it does not make a container breach impossible.
Always rotate secrets frequently and avoid long-lived credentials.

Runtime security tools
Even after i d x _ 3 f c 4 8 e b 9 scanning and hardening, your container environment is vulnerable at runtime. Attackers may exploit
zero-day flaws, escalate privileges, or pivot inside a running container. Static scanning can only guard against
known threats. Runtime security tools act as a detective and safety net, observing behavior in real time and alerting
on anomalies that signal attacks, misconfigurations, or suspicious activity.

Chapter 13 442
In this section, we will do the following:
Explain the role and architecture of runtime security
Introduce Falco as a leading open source solution
Walk through the deployment of Falco in a local or containerized environment
Demonstrate writing or customizing a detection rule
Show how alerts can feed into response workflows
Discuss trade-offs and deployment considerations
Let's begin.
Why runtime security matters
Runtime security i d x _ c f 1 2 d 3 5 7 is essential because many security risks only manifest while a container is running, making
continuous observation and behavioral analysis a critical complement to build-time and deployment-time
controls. The key reasons include the following:
Zero-day and unknown threats: Not all vulnerabilities are known at scan time. A runtime exploit may
bypass prior defenses.
Configuration drift and runtime changes: Containers may misbehave, mount unexpected volumes, or
spawn child processes you didn't anticipate.
Behavioral detection: Monitoring system calls, process execution, and file access reveals abnormal
behavior such as privilege escalation, spawning shells, or modifying binaries.
Forensics and audit trail: Runtime tools provide visibility into what actually happened, which helps in
incident investigation and root cause analysis.
Static tools enforce don't deploy bad stuff. Runtime tools say: if something bad is happening now, catch it. They
complement one another.
Introducing Falco
Falco i d x _ a 2 f e 3 8 7 3 is a mature, cloud-native runtime security and threat i d x _ 9 9 3 2 d a 1 d detection tool.
Here are the key i d x _ 2 a c 7 3 9 4 6 concepts and architecture:
Event collection: Falco listens to kernel events, such as syscalls, via extended Berkeley Packet Filter
(eBPF) probes i d x _ 9 6 d c 7 8 0 c or kernel modules.
Rules engine: Events are evaluated against a set of rules (written in YAML) that express suspicious
patterns (e.g., execution of a shell in a container, write to /etc/passwd, or network activity from
unexpected binaries).
Alerts and outputs: When a rule is triggered, Falco emits an alert via stdout, logs, webhooks, or
integration with other systems.
Contextual metadata: Falco enriches alerts with metadata (container ID, image name, namespace, etc.),
helping you map behavior to specific workloads.
Falco is typically deployed as a daemon (or DaemonSet in Kubernetes), watching all runtime activity continuously.

Deploying Falco in a Docker environment
Let's run a i d x _ 6 4 4 8 8 f a 3 simple Falco instance alongside your containers for experimentation. Later, you can adopt more
hardened deployment models:
Pull the Falco container image:
$ docker pull falcosecurity/falco:latest
Run Falco with required mounts and privileges. Here's a command using fully privileged mode, which is

$ docker run --rm -it \
--privileged \
-v /var/run/docker.sock:/host/var/run/docker.sock \
-v /proc:/host/proc:ro \
-v /etc:/host/etc:ro \
falcosecurity/falco:latest
Here are some details to the above command:
--privileged gives Falco broad kernel access
The /proc and /etc host paths are mounted read-only so Falco can inspect them
The Docker socket is mounted so Falco can map container events
Once i d x _ a 0 2 8 d b 0 9 running, Falco will begin monitoring system events and printing alerts in real time when rules are
violated.
Try triggering an alert. In another shell, start an innocuous container:
$ docker run --rm alpine /bin/sh \
-c "touch /etc/passwd"
Because writing to /etc is suspicious inside a container, Falco may flag this action. Check Falco's output to
see a rule violation, with metadata indicating which container, process, and command triggered it.
Customizing detection rules
Out of the box, Falco i d x _ e 7 e 5 b 9 b 4 ships with a default rule set covering common behaviors, such as SSH invocation, suspicious
file writes, and process execution.
You will often need to adjust or write rules tailored to your environment. Here's an example rule you might add to
watch for shells spawned in containers:
